biggestGap: You cannot tell what any man on the board is. The top-down play camera that fixed the occlusion spent the one cue that was left. Projecting up to 900 vertices per mesh through the live camera at 1920x804, White's back rank draws: rook 98.8x85.5 px, knight 76.3x90.4, bishop 73.0x80.6, queen 67.4x79.9, king 71.2x86.0, pawn 80.1x76.5 — against world heights of 3.07 / 3.20 / 3.55 / 4.14 / 4.56 / 2.57 m. The ordering is not compressed, it is INVERTED: a 2.57 m pawn draws 80.1 px wide and the 4.14 m queen 67.4; the 3.20 m knight draws 90.4 px tall and the 4.56 m king 86.0. At 80 degrees of declination almost nothing of a man's height reaches the screen, so what is left is a plan-view footprint that is the same chamfered hexagon for all six types, and apparent size is set by WHERE a piece stands, not what it is. The image test says the same thing without reference to geometry: crop the eight men of rank 1 at 80x80 from refs/renders/play-critic.png, normalise each to zero mean and unit variance so exposure cannot fake a difference, and take mean absolute difference. Two men of the SAME type average 0.945 apart (RR 1.138, NN 0.875, BB 0.823) while two of DIFFERENT types average 0.819 — LESS. King against bishop is 0.533, the most similar pair on the rank; every different-type pair on the board is closer than the two rooks are to each other. The 20-px SVG glyph in the HUD tray reads instantly as a queen, a bishop, a knight. The 76-px carved model on the board does not. Nothing else on screen closes the gap: there are no rank/file coordinates anywhere (the Record panel prints 'Nxc2' and nothing tells you where c2 is), and interactive.ts never marks the engine's from/to squares — aff.setSelection / setDestinations / setCheck are the only board marks, and all three fire only for YOUR move.
critiqueDetail:
THE GUARANTEE IS INTACT AND WAS TESTED AGAINST THIS ROUND'S TREE — 9 files modified, 790 insertions, plus 6 new source modules (playview.ts, reclaim.ts, glyphs.ts, readout.ts, grade-play.ts, view.ts). king-surrender at t=2.8 returns md5 45ebe28f78b6837bb2816b5fcccbe9ab at 2,264,723 bytes: the exact hash and byte count rounds 3, 4 and 5 recorded. wide-establishing at t=3 captured twice is cmp-clean byte-identical, md5 f64e1f7eee0c9fa66f15630a3334c5f8 at 2,630,788 bytes, the same as rounds 4 and 5. verify-mate is 3/3 with legalReplies=0 on all three lines. The isolation is by construction rather than by luck: isPlayView() gates on WHICH SHOT is aimed, so grade-play.ts and the clamped chamber can only be reached by 'play' or by interactive, and PLAY_CAM_MIN_Y=18.0 sits 7.4 m above the highest camera in SHOTS.

Q2 — CAN YOU SEE THE BOARD? YES, COMPLETELY, AND I TRIED HARD TO BREAK IT. I projected all 64 square centres through window.__WC__.world.camera and cast a ray from the camera position to each one, against every visible mesh in the scene (239 targets at 1600x900), counting any first hit that was not the board group itself. Result at 1600x900: 0 squares off-screen, 0 blocked by scenery, 32 blocked by the piece standing on them — which is the only correct answer. I then re-ran it on a FRESH PAGE at four more aspect ratios, because main.ts derives vertical FOV from a fixed horizontal extent and a different aspect is a different frustum: 1920x804 (fov 38.0), 1366x768 (fov 49.6), 2560x1080 (fov 38.3), 1280x1024 (fov 66.7). Every one: 0 off-screen, 0 scenery-blocked, 32 piece-blocked. Then the pieces themselves — 32 men, 9 sample points each on their world bounding boxes (crown, mid, four sides, base, two shoulders), 288 rays: 0 scenery hits and 0 sample points outside the frustum, at every viewport. Round 2's failure was White's rank 1 sitting 20-23 px BELOW the bottom edge; rank 1 now lands at y=736 of 900 at 1600x900 and y=628 of 768 at 1366x768. The piers-and-screens clamp in playview.ts works, and it works without emptying the near field — the corners of refs/renders/play-critic.png are still stone.

Q3 — IS IT BLOWN OUT? NO, NOT ON THE TIER A DESKTOP GETS. metrics.mjs on refs/renders/play-critic.png: fracBlown 0.00089, medianLuminance 0.1216. The cinematic control, /tmp/k.png (king-surrender) through the same tool: fracBlown 0.02418, medianLuminance 0.1059. The play frame is 27x LESS blown than the film frame at essentially the same median — the film shot is the blown one, by design. Whole-frame numbers can hide a hot centre, so I cropped to the board itself using the projected square centres. Board (x 613-1298, y 104-753, 444,565 px): median 0.1822, p99 0.7916, p999 0.8728, max 0.9338, fracBlown 0, and 0.042% of pixels above L 0.90. Middle 4x4 only (x 827-1084, y 307-550, 62,451 px): median 0.2052, p99 0.7394, max 0.8041 — 205 of 255 — with ZERO pixels above 0.90 and zero clipped channels. grade-play.ts records the before as cream squares at median 139, p99 222, peak 225; the middle of the board now peaks at 205 and nothing in it goes above 230. The complaint is fixed.

BUT THE FIX IS HIGH-TIER ONLY, AND I HAVE A CLEAN CONTROL FOR IT. lighting/index.ts line 289 reads `high ? (play ? PlayGradeShader : GradeShader) : LowGradeShader` — the play grade's highlight knee does not exist below 'high'. Same shot, same t, same FEN (a white pawn on e5), only --quality changed: the pawn crop (80x80 at 960,335) is median 0.651 / p99 0.794 / max 0.812 with ZERO pixels over 0.90 at high, and median 0.853 / max 0.939 with 27.9% of its pixels over 0.90 at low. The whole board region goes fracBlown 0.00006 -> 0.01444, a factor of 241. Live on the low tier it is worse than the capture: playing a real capture at 1280x720 and screenshotting after the wreckage cleared, the pawn standing on e5 measured median luminance 0.988 with 79.8% of its pixels above 0.98 — a featureless white plinth. Desktop defaults to 'high' so a desktop player does not see this; a phone does, and interactiveQuality() sends phones to 'low' by definition.

Q4 — DOES DEBRIS CLEAR? YES. I set up a forced capture (dxe5) from a FEN and sampled the scene every ~3 s for 314 s. Baseline 170 meshes / 89 visible / 0 under 'destruction' / 62 geometries. The blast lands at scene t=0.48 and takes it to 200 / 118 / 30 / 92 — exactly +30 meshes and +30 geometries. It then holds flat at 30 for 4.3 scene seconds (63 consecutive samples, scene 0.48 to 4.77 — reclaim.ts requires a body to be SLEEPING, and maxAge is 3.0 s). At scene 4.82 it starts going and the sequence is 30, 28, 27, 25, 23, 22, 19, 15, 14, 10, 9, 5, 3, 1 — the whole heap over 1.1 scene seconds, near edge first, ending 5.4 s after the blast. VISIBLE mesh count returns to EXACTLY the baseline 89. Confirmed visually: refs/renders/debris-t1.png has a white rubble field over three squares and refs/renders/debris-final.png has clean marble. ONE FRAGMENT IS STRANDED. Total meshes settle at 171 against a baseline of 170, geometries at 63 against 62, and the 'destruction' group holds 1 visible mesh — flat for 0.9 scene seconds and 36 wall seconds after everything else had gone. One leaked mesh and one leaked geometry per capture is not a frame cost, but over a 30-capture game it is 30 shards lying on the marble that nothing will ever take away.

Q5 — CAN YOU READ THE SCORE? YES, AND THIS IS THE ROUND'S BEST WORK. I played 12 white moves by clicking the real canvas at 1280x720: 1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 e6 3.Bc4 d5 4.Nc3 dxc4 5.d4 cxd3 6.O-O Nb4 7.Ng5 Nxc2 8.Qh5 Qd7 9.Nxe6 Qxe6 10.Qxf7+ Qxf7 11.Rb1 Bc5 12.Bg5 h6 — 24 plies, 7 captures, an en passant, castling, and a check. Every move was accepted; 11 of the 12 in 1.2 s of wall clock from first click to accepted move (the first was 17.6 s, which is worker spin-up), and the engine answered every one in about 2.0 s. Zero page errors and zero console errors across the whole game. Then I screenshotted it (refs/renders/play-hud.png) and read it: Black's tablet says BLACK / THE ENGINE / +15 with a tray of queen, bishop, knight, pawn, pawn and the word WAITING; White's says WHITE / YOU with two pawns and an ember beside TO MOVE; the Record panel lists all twelve numbered pairs in SAN with h6 in orange as the last move. I recomputed the material independently from the move list — Black took Q+B+N+P+P=17, White took two pawns — and +15 is exactly right, as is every glyph in both trays. Whose turn it is, what each side has taken, and who is ahead are all answerable from the screen without touching the console. Round 3's critic had to read the FEN out of the JS console to pick a move; that bar is cleared and then some.

THREE SMALLER THINGS, ALL MEASURED. (1) Fresh wreckage is the brightest object in the game. Sampled in refs/renders/debris-t1.png, the rubble from one capture has a lit luminance of 0.980 and a peak of 0.991, against 0.635 for a white pawn and 0.347 for a black piece; inside the rubble crop 13.9% of pixels are above 0.98 and 53.6% above 0.90, median 0.906. For the four seconds it lasts, the thing that just happened is a white flare over three squares and the two men standing next to it are the dimmer objects. (2) The quality tier is decided once at boot and never revisited. interactiveQuality() reads pointer/hover/deviceMemory only, world.quality is read in nine modules and written nowhere else, and the resolution ladder bottoms out at max(0.75, 800/cssWidth) — so a desktop whose GPU cannot hold the high tier has no fallback at all and at most a 44% pixel saving available. Under this box's software rasteriser the desktop tier renders at a median 17,744 ms/frame (25 frames, min 16,976, max 24,795) behind a 1200x675 buffer at a 1600x900 canvas; that number is the rasteriser, not a GPU, but it is exactly the case a fallback would exist for and there is none. (3) The board is 18-29% of a desktop screen — 541x511 px of 1366x768 (26.4%), 920x873 of 2560x1080 (29.0%), 506x479 of 1280x1024 (18.5%). Squares come out 63-115 px, which is a normal online-chess size, so this is not too small so much as very surrounded.

history.gap: none — 3/3 demo lines verified as real checkmate with zero legal replies

The play camera crops White's own back rank off the bottom of the frame — all eight rank-1 square centres sit 20-23 px below the canvas edge, leaving a 22-28 px sliver, so clicking where your own knight or king appears to be does nothing. Deterministic at every window size, and it hits on move 2.

You cannot tell what any piece is by looking at it. Every piece is the same pale armoured figure from behind and only height separates the types: rook 119.2 px, knight 132.2 px, bishop 141.1 px on screen — 13.0 px and 8.8 px apart, 7-11 percent of their own height, with no colour, crest or marking to help. It survives at full capture resolution, so it is not the software renderer. I picked all nine of my moves by reading the FEN out of the JS console; and since the HUD never prints state.lastMove, you also cannot tell what the engine just played.

The 32 carved pieces. They are 354,599 of the 404,665 triangles the phone submits every frame (87.6%), 56 of its 117 draw calls, and 1,065 ms of a 1,919 ms frame (55%) — measured by hiding exactly those 32 groups at a fixed 800x370 buffer and timing with a readPixels fence: 1,919 -> 854 ms, 117 -> 61 calls, 404,665 -> 50,066 triangles. The board, which this round rebuilt, is now 5 calls, 11,746 triangles and 296 ms; the chamber is 34 calls and 420 ms. src/pieces is the one module the round did not open. Every figure is uniquely carved, so nothing is instanced or merged; there is one body mesh plus one arm mesh per piece, no LOD of any kind, and a pawn 30 m away at the top of the frame carries the same ~11,000 triangles as the king a metre from the lens. 64 carved geometries are resident for the 32 men actually on the board.

The stone fragment shader on the 32 pieces. With geometry, draw calls (93), triangles (139,298) and screen coverage all held EXACTLY constant and only the piece material swapped, the frame is: shipped stone 1,717 ms / MeshStandard 1,317 / MeshLambert 1,083 / MeshBasic unlit 950 / pieces hidden 850. So of the 867 ms the pieces cost, rasterising them unlit is 100 ms (11%), lighting them over the 21 punctual lights is 133-367 ms, and the custom stone GLSL is ~400 ms ON TOP of PBR and ~767 ms over unlit — 45% of the whole frame, the single largest item left. The frame is fragment-bound and still is: through the app's own path at 0.116 / 0.189 / 0.314 Mpx it costs 850 / 1,217 / 1,767 ms, i.e. ~317 ms fixed plus 4,610 ms per megapixel, against round 4's 4,780 ms/Mpx. Cutting piece triangles 2.90x did not move that slope, because triangles were never what the slope was made of.
